newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Paris suburb has tough words for election hopefuls.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Paris suburb has tough words for election hopefuls.

text.p: Jeanine, a native-born resident of the tough Paris suburb of Sarcelles, has a sober warning for France's political establishment, which is preparing for a parliamentary election later this month.
"The parties are all the same," she said while shopping on a Saturday morning. "If things continue the way they are, we'll have to vote for the National Front."

"I'm serious," said Jeanine, a married, retired woman in her fifties, who has voted for both left and right, but never for Jean-Marie Le Pen's extreme-right, anti-immigrant movement. She was now contemplating that step "to see if anything changes".
Her alienation from the political centre sums up a deep sense of disenchantment and detachment widely felt in this and other disadvantaged high-rise suburbs.

Disillusioned by Socialist rule under the late president Francois Mitterrand and bitter about rising joblessness under the present centre-right coalition, many residents of what used to be called the "red belt" display a deep political apathy.
"We got cheated by the right and we may get cheated again by the left," said self-declared Socialist Armand Heun, 86, who has lived in Sarcelles since 1911.
Sarcelles and neighboring Garges are typical of the capital's poor outlying communities, with block after block of grim subsidised apartment buildings surrounded by urban sprawl.
APATHY RULES AMONG YOUNG RESIDENTS OF FORMER "RED BELT"
Some 95 nationalities and ethnic groups live side by side in these isolated districts -- separated from the Paris of fashion, museums and fine dining by the "peripherique" ring road.
Young residents, with little hope of either a job or higher education, turn easily to vandalism, drugs and crime.
"It doesn't interest me," said Patrick Ulmany, a black teenager in Garges who would be voting in his first election -- if he did.
Asked whether he intended to cast his ballot, he shrugged, pulled his baseball cap over his eyes and said: "They're all windbags. All they do is lie. It won't make any difference."
That bitterness is not limited to jobless youths. It has spread from the ranks of immigrants and the unemployed to parts of society usually considered within the political mainstream.

"All those who are standing, on the left, on the right, in the middle, etc...pffft!," scoffed Marie, who lives in the more middle-class Yvelines area west of Paris, but came to Sarcelles for its colourful Saturday market.

Marie recalled a letter President Jacques Chirac sent voters before the 1995 presidential election full of high-sounding pledges. "We've had plenty of promises, but as for the rest...," she tailed off without saying if or how she would vote.
Dominique Strauss-Kahn, mayor of Sarcelles and Socialist candidate for its parliamentary seat, said that what residents of this and other suburbs want is jobs, security and clean streets.

On a campaign tour through the old village of Sarcelles, Strauss-Kahn, an economic expert and potential finance minister, shrugged and laughed when asked if any of the town's residents ever talked to him about Europe or its planned single currency.
"It's all local issues," he said. "Jobs, safety and cleanliness in the streets."
Chirac dissolved parliament and called a snap parliamentary election 10 months early for May 25 and June 1, saying France needed a "new elan" to pursue European integration.
Gaullist Prime Minister Alain Juppe has led the government's campaign, saying a win by the left would lead to more taxes, more deficits, more illegal immigration and less security.
The Socialists, capitalising on Juppe's deep unpopularity, have warned that a conservative victory would keep the prime minister in power and lead to harsher austerity.
MANY IN SARCELLES FAVOUR SOCIALISTS
In Garges and Sarcelles, where daily life is punctuated by conflict with the police and violent crime, many residents respond to the Socialist pitch.

"I want the left in power because if we have Juppe for five more years, it will be austerity, austerity," said Gilberte Lentin, a long-time resident of Garges who was born in the overseas department of French Guiana in South America.
French economic growth has stagnated over the last two years as the conservative government has struggled to cut spending and deficits to qualify for a single European currency.
Unemployment, an already painful 11.7 percent when Chirac won election in May 1995 on a promise to bring it down, has risen to a record 12.8 percent.
The jobless rate in Sarcelles is 15 percent, well above the national average, local officials said.
"The most important thing is work, to develop the French economy," Lentin said. Her own sons cannot find jobs, she said.
Eighteen-year-old Cecilie Conhoc, whose parents moved to Paris from Guadeloupe 30 years ago, said she felt Juppe had not addressed her concerns and she would vote against him.

"The government should take care of us a bit more. We are not the elite, but we are human beings and Mr Juppe should hear that," said Conhoc, a language student who will be voting for the first time on May 25.
"He mainly talks to the elite of the country but he must remember that it's thanks to people like us in the streets that he has been elected."
European integration and a single currency, two of the main grounds Chirac gave for calling the vote, are barely mentioned.
In extensive interviews, no one brought up European issues spontaneously. When prompted, many said they took second place to local concerns.

Echoing the Socialist stance that there should be no further austerity to prepare for monetary union, Lentin said: "I want the single currency but not at any price. We must first restore the French economy so there is not so much misery."
